title: Not yet
hookLine: Ananda was still unawakened when the Buddha died, and wept

lines: SOME FREE, SOME ON THE WAY.
cards: Night, in a grove of sal trees at Kusinara. The Buddha is dying. Around him are monks of every kind: some, the texts say, fully free, and some still on the way.
Ananda is among the second group. He has been at the teacher's side for many years, and kept what he heard. And he is not yet awakened.
Earlier on this path we watched him slip away to weep in a doorway, and the Buddha call him back. Today, stay with the two words under the whole scene: not yet.

teach.b: First, the start, long before. In the Samyutta Nikaya, Ananda remembers that when he was newly ordained, a monk named Punna taught him, and hearing it, he broke through to the teaching.
So Ananda had entered the path early. On this night he wasn't a beginner. He was a learner.
Second, the learner at the end. The Pali word is sekha: one still in training, on the path but not at its end.

teach.h: STILL A LEARNER AT THE END.
teach.b: In the doorway, Ananda says it of himself, in paraphrase: I'm still a learner, with work left to do, and my teacher, who was so kind to me, is passing away. The Buddha doesn't call that failure.
He tells Ananda he has served him well, and says: keep at it, and you'll soon be free. Soon. Not now.
Third, the night itself. When the Buddha passes, the discourse says some monks weep and some bear it calmly: everything made comes apart. Ananda speaks a verse about the shock of that moment.

teach.h: A NIGHT OF TALK WITH ANURUDDHA.
teach.b: And then, the text says, Anuruddha, one of the monks already free, and Ananda spent the rest of that night together, talking about the teaching. The finished one and the unfinished one, side by side until morning.
In the texts, the learner is already on the path and counted among the noble disciples.
Ananda had kept what he heard, served his teacher faithfully, and still wasn't done, and the story treats that as a place to stand rather than a verdict. Tomorrow, how not yet ended.

how: In Theravada teaching, a sekha or learner is a disciple who has entered the path but not completed it, and Ananda's story is told to encourage practitioners who are still on the way.

o: never able to reach the goal in this life
still a learner, on the path but not at its end
too new to the teaching to understand it

p: taught Ananda when he was new

s: Ananda was fully awakened when the Buddha died
he was still a learner, on the path but not at its end.
the Buddha scolded Ananda for still being a learner
he said Ananda had served him well and would soon be free.
after the passing, Anuruddha and Ananda talked about the teaching for the rest of the night
the free one and the learner, side by side until morning.

games.q: you're Ananda. the teacher has just died. some monks are weeping, and Anuruddha, already free, is calm. what do you do with the rest of the night?
o: go off alone with your grief.
sit with Anuruddha and talk about the teaching.
act as calm as Anuruddha, whatever you feel.
games.why: the discourse says Anuruddha and Ananda spent the rest of that night together, talking about the teaching.

practice: Name one thing in your life that's still unfinished, a habit, a skill, a grief, and say it plainly, then add two words: not yet.
Then, the way the Buddha did for Ananda, name one thing you have already done well, and hold both with the breath.

wordCard.voice: Not yet. When the Buddha died, Ananda was still a learner, on the path and not at its end, and he wept; the Buddha's word for him was soon. Today's word.

orig.note: Pali: a learner, one in training; a disciple who has entered the path but not finished it.

carryVoice: Your line: soon, not now. Not yet isn't never, and nobody sent the learner away. That's day seven hundred thirty-six.

sources.ref: Digha Nikaya 16 (Mahaparinibbana Sutta), Ananda as learner; the passing; Anuruddha and Ananda through the night
